extracted.intended_audience: instrument makers and experimental electricians building carbon-button telephones, microphones, and tasimeters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for designing, manufacturing, adjusting, and wiring carbon-button transmitters, microphone-like transmitters, and tasimeters so they reproduce speech, detect small pressure/temperature changes, and operate reliably on telegraph/telephone lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduce intensity and quality by varying current strength
rubrics_metrics.description: A transmitter must vary the strength of the electric current in exact accordance with the tone to be transmitted in order to reproduce intensity and quality as well as pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gray's device (rod dipping into acidulated water) varied resistance inversely with sound intensity, allowing reproduction of multiple simultaneous tones without losing character; Reis's circuit-breaker reproduced pitch only because current strength remained constant (anti-pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pressure-sensitive semi-conductors for transmitters
rubrics_metrics.description: Select materials (semi-conductors) whose resistance varies with applied pressure so diaphragm vibrations translate into current variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edison's insight: semi-conductors vary resistance with pressure. Practical implementation: place a spring-faced platinum contact against a semi-conducting cup and adjust by screw so diaphragm pressure changes contact pressure and thus resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material selection ranking for carbon buttons
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer materials in this order for carbon-button transmitters: 1. lampblack; 2. hyperoxide of lead; 3. iodide of copper; 4. graphite; 5. gas-carbon; 6. platinum-black.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lampblack is highest value because its particles are most finely divided, producing the largest change in resistance for a given pressure. Coarser materials (gas-carbon, graphite) are less sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lampblack production and selection requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain lampblack deposited at the lowest possible temperature and untouched by flame; reject commercial lampblack and brown portions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: take chimney lampblack, lay on white slab, remove brown portions, grind, press at several thousand pounds in a mold, repowder and repress several times, and finally mold into buttons weighing ~300 mg each. Failure to use properly produced lampblack yields excessive resistance and unusable buttons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target electrical resistance values for circuit tuning
rubrics_metrics.description: Tune the circuit so the overall circuit resistance is very small compared to the button's normal resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best arrangement found: make the resistance of the circuit 1/4 of an ohm while the normal resistance of the carbon itself was about 3 ohms. This makes the pressure-induced relative change in resistance significant to the line current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Button geometry and mounting (carbon 'button')
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a small circular 'button' of carbon placed between two platinum disks with electrical connection and mechanical support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rubber tubing to ensure electrical contact between disks and button during experiments; properly armature the button to avoid violent shocks which would accelerate friability. If cracked, volume is not materially lessened, but armaturing prevents unnecessary damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff: sensitivity versus durability (hardening the button)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardening treatments can increase durability but tend to impair the delicacy (sensitivity) of the button.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to harden by mixing other substances and high-temperature treatments make buttons less delicate; balance required depending on expected mechanical shock and lifetime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diaphragm design and damping for articulation and volume
rubrics_metrics.description: Diaphragm choice (delicate vibrating, damped, or heavy rigid) directly affects articulation and loudness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubber damping: reduces lingering vibration but tends to muffle sound and flattens with use (anti-pattern). Spiral metallic spring: initial springs produced extraneous tones; thicker wire reduced tone. Best result: heavy rigid diaphragm fastened to carbon disk (no vibration) — yields perfect articulation and greatly increased volume because larger area produces greater pressure on the carbon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical materials whose thermal expansion disturbs operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use handle or parts that expand/contract enough to change pressure on the carbon button during normal temperature variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubber handles caused tardy pressure changes and flattening; iron handles produced molecular-action noises due to expansion. Edison dispensed with the handle altogether to avoid such disturbances and discovered micro-tasimeter applications from this sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple carbon disks: volume vs articulation tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding several carbon disks increases volume but degrades articulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments with multiple disks showed louder output but worse speech clarity; choose configuration according to whether loudness or intelligibility is primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect/non-homogeneous contacts as transmitter principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Transmitters that rely on imperfect contacts or non-homogeneous fillings (powders, impregnated particles) change contact resistance under vibration and can act as sensitive transmitters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hughes' tube filled with white silver powder (tin/zinc) whose contact resistance changes under tensile/compressive strain; mercury-impregnated carbon; crude arrangements like a loose nail across two nails can transmit sounds. Essential: the substance/contact must be non-homogeneous to allow variable particle contacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro-tasimeter adjustment and sensitivity setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Set initial pressure so the galvanometer needle deflects a few degrees; once settled, smallest pressure changes are indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For extreme delicacy, use a Thomson reflecting galvanometer in a Wheatstone bridge with the tasimeter in one arm and the other three resistances equal; minute resistance changes at tasimeter show on the galvanometer. Use micrometer screw to return needle to zero and read expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tasimeter uses and measurement procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the carbon-button tasimeter to detect small quantities of heat, determine coefficients of expansion, and measure hygrometric changes by substituting appropriate test materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure examples: in eclipse observations the tasimeter detected corona heat; to determine coefficient of expansion attach micrometer-screw arrangement and read turns required to null galvanometer change. For hygrometry, insert a material that changes volume with moisture and read galvanometer change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical design to limit unwanted thermal input
rubrics_metrics.description: When measuring thermal effects, shield the test piece so only desired heat reaches it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include funnel-shaped opening with a small slit facing the test sample to cut off unwanted heat; use protective tubes (silver tube inside brass tube) in micro-tasimeter variants to control thermal coupling and exploit differential expansion between dissimilar metals for measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit arrangement for loud-speaking telephone with motograph receiver
rubrics_metrics.description: Use induction coil with primary, secondary, and tertiary circuits; include relay, bells, push-buttons to manage ringing and talking connections; arrange push-button contacts to protect motograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When initiating a call, bell-button completes line through receiver relay to ring the other station. Depress push-button to connect primary and tertiary completing local primary circuit through transmitter; tertiary kept closed so the other party may interrupt. Alternate contact of primary and tertiary at push-button prevents simultaneous knocks that would disrupt the motograph chalk cylinder. Use one Callaud cell for talking, two for bell; a small electric engine can replace a crank for motograph drive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design consideration for line conditions and interference
rubrics_metrics.description: Carbon telephones, using stronger currents and less sensitive receivers, are less affected by inductive disturbance from neighboring wires and can operate over longer distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments showed carbon telephone successful over 100–200 miles and even up to 720 miles on certain lines; it can be used on Morse circuits with many way-stations and on wires simultaneously used for quadruplex transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver matching and use of electro-motograph
rubrics_metrics.description: Pair the carbon transmitter with appropriate receivers (e.g., electro-motograph) and induction-coil arrangements to maximize efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edison's recommended arrangement: carbon transmitter in primary local circuit, induction coil with secondary/tertiary to line and receiver; use motograph receiver for loud-speaking applications and manage contact timing to avoid damaging the motograph surface.
